title: 2 Samuel 6:16–23
context: 2 Samuel 6:16–23 shows the ark set in the tent David pitched for it, with burnt offerings, peace offerings, a blessing in the LORD’s name, and gifts of food for all the people. Michal, Saul’s daughter, watches David dancing and despises him. When he returns to bless his household, she mocks him for uncovering himself before the servant girls. David answers that he celebrated before the LORD, who chose him over her father, and that he will become even more undignified. The narrator closes by noting that Michal had no child to the day of her death. Both traditions read the scene within the conflict between the houses of Saul and David and the theme of humble worship before the LORD, and they avoid importing later debates into it.

verses.text: As the LORD’s ark came into David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart.
verses.arminianNotes: As the ark enters David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul sees David leaping and dancing before the LORD and despises him in her heart. Arminians note that the narrator calls her "the daughter of Saul," which places her response within the conflict between Saul’s house and David’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the text describes her inner contempt before she speaks. Both traditions read the verse as narrative, without pressing it into later debates about worship styles, and they recognize the painful history between Michal and David (1 Samuel 18–19; 2 Samuel 3:13–16).

verses.text: They brought in the LORD’s ark, and set it in its place in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it; and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: They set the LORD’s ark in the tent David pitched, and David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. Arminians see David providing a place for God’s presence in the capital and leading the people in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that this tent is distinct from the tabernacle, which 1 Chronicles 16:39 places at Gibeon. Both traditions see the verse as preparing for David’s desire to build a house for the LORD in chapter 7.

verses.text: When David had finished offering the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: After the offerings, David blesses the people in the name of the LORD of Armies. Arminians see the king acting as a servant who brings God’s blessing to the people, which fits the shepherd role described in 5:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the parallel with Solomon blessing the people at the temple dedication (1 Kings 8:14). Both traditions see the verse as showing the king’s role in leading the nation in worship under God’s name.

verses.text: He gave to all the people, even among the whole multitude of Israel, both to men and women, to everyone a portion of bread, dates, and raisins. So all the people departed, each to his own house.
verses.arminianNotes: David gives bread, dates, and raisins to every man and woman in Israel, and the people go home. Arminians see generosity that includes everyone, men and women alike, in the celebration of God’s presence among them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The exact meaning of two of the food words is uncertain. Both traditions read the gifts as a festive meal that shares the joy of the day with the whole people, consistent with the peace offerings.

verses.text: Then David returned to bless his household. Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, “How glorious the king of Israel was today, who uncovered himself today in the eyes of his servants’ maids, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!”
verses.arminianNotes: David returns to bless his household, and Michal mocks him for uncovering himself before the servants’ maids like a shameless fool. Arminians read her words as contempt for David’s humility, which she sees as beneath a king’s dignity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that "uncovered" likely refers to dancing in the simple linen ephod rather than full royal dress. Both traditions read the exchange as narrative about pride and humility, not as a general rule about dress or worship.

verses.text: David said to Michal, “It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father, and above all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of the LORD, over Israel. Therefore I will celebrate before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: David answers that he celebrated before the LORD, who chose him over her father and his house to be prince over Israel. Arminians see David grounding his worship in God’s choice and grace, which makes him willing to be humbled before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that David’s identity rests on God’s choosing, so he does not need to guard his dignity. Both traditions read the verse as showing that worship is directed to God, not to human observers.

verses.text: I will be yet more undignified than this, and will be worthless in my own sight. But the maids of whom you have spoken will honor me.”
verses.arminianNotes: David says he will be even more undignified and lowly in his own eyes, but the maids will honor him. Arminians see a humble spirit that cares more about honoring God than about appearances, and they see the maids’ honor as a reversal of Michal’s contempt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and connect the verse with the biblical theme that God exalts the humble (1 Samuel 2:7–8). Both traditions read David’s words as worship-centered humility, not as license for carelessness in worship.

verses.text: Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
verses.arminianNotes: Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death. Arminians note that the text does not say whether this was divine judgment, David’s choice, or circumstances, and they avoid claiming more than the narrator says.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the cause is not stated. Many note that the verse means Saul’s line will not continue through a son of David and Michal. Both traditions read it as a sober close to the scene and avoid modern framing.
